extracted.intended_audience: advanced readers of philosophy and literary criticism (students, scholars, reflective writers)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and first-principles for constructing or judging philosophical systems: what counts as knowledge, the place of intuition and self-consciousness, methodological postulates, and the separation of subjective vs objective inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophic imagination / intuitive knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Only those who can interpret symbols and possess an inner faculty acquire the philosophic imagination or 'sacred power of self-intuition'; this faculty reveals correspondences (e.g., wings forming in a caterpillar) that exceed mere notional understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/metaphors (caterpillar/chrysalis, air-sylph) illustrate that intuition is a living organ of spirit present in some but not all; the notional understanding is only a shadow of living truth and cannot substitute for intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy is not universally intelligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy cannot be made fully intelligible to all, even to the learned, because its first principles aim to render the mind intuitive of the spiritual and require an inwardly disciplined consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reader must be prepared to 'rest dissatisfied with imperfect light' only until impossibility of fuller knowledge is shown; lack of inner organ makes philosophy appear as mere play of words to many.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical method requires a postulate / primitive intuition
rubrics_metrics.description: Like geometry, philosophy must commence from a primary, postulated construction or intuition (a 'first productive act' for the inner sense) rather than from a demonstrable proposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The postulate functions as a practical idea to generate further evidence; one must decide what the most original construction of the inner sense is (direction of the inner sense is often an act of freedom).

rubrics_metrics.name: Purification by scientific scepticism (methodological restraint)
rubrics_metrics.description: Transcendental/philosophical inquiry demands voluntary, scientific scepticism to exclude innate prejudices and to prevent illegitimate interpolations of foreign principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Descartes' method of doubt; natural philosophers must exclude arbitrariness, occult qualities, final causes where inappropriate; the aim is an 'absolute and scientific scepticism' to secure future certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strict separation of natural and transcendental philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: Each pole (natural/ objective vs transcendental/ subjective) must adhere to its own principles and exclude the other's assumptions to avoid confusion and mutilation of inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural philosophers avoid subjective interpolations (occult agents, final causes); transcendental philosophers avoid supposing objective impresses (brain pictures of retina). Maintaining this purity is essential for success in each science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth is correlative to being (Thesis I)
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge without a corresponding reality is not genuine knowledge: truth presupposes a corresponding being (to know implies that there is something known).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is stated as a foundational axiom: to know is essentially a relation between representation and an existent correlate.

rubrics_metrics.name: All truth is either mediate or immediate (Thesis II)
rubrics_metrics.description: Truths are either immediate/original (absolute, A = A) or mediate/derived (their certainty depends on other truths, represented as B → A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chains of truths without a first (a series without a first) are absurd; mediate truths require a self-grounded truth to supply certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for a self-grounded absolute truth (Thesis III)
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy must posit an absolute, self-grounded truth — a principle that is its own predicate and requires no antecedent cause — to supply unconditional certainty to other positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a principle must preclude the possibility of requiring a cause or antecedent; it functions as the staple or central principle giving stability to a system of truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness of the absolute principle (Thesis IV)
rubrics_metrics.description: There can be only one self-grounded absolute principle; multiple such principles would each require reference to another and thus fail to be self-established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This can be shown a priori (logical incompatibility of multiple absolutes) and a posteriori when the discovered principle demonstrates universal antecedents in its conception.

rubrics_metrics.name: The absolute principle cannot be an ordinary thing/object (Thesis V)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ultimate principle cannot be a thing or object because every thing is what it is by reference to other things (contingent), and an object is inconceivable without a subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An infinite independent 'thing' is a contradiction (like an infinite circle); thus the principle must not be exclusively object or subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: The absolute principle is the identity of subject and object — the I AM / self (Thesis VI)
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle is the identity of subject and object manifest in the I AM (self, spirit, self-consciousness), where object and subject, being and knowing, are identical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as a perpetual self-duplication: a subject that constructs itself objectively while remaining a subject; all other predicates must be modes or repetitions of this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-knowledge is immediate; self-consciousness is the essential predicate (Thesis VII)
rubrics_metrics.description: If we know ourselves only through ourselves, the only proper predicate of self is self-consciousness; in self-consciousness spirit attains identity of object and representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequently, the spirit (in viewing objects) views only itself; immediate intuitive knowledge is thus grounded in self-consciousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intelligence/self-consciousness presupposes will and freedom (Thesis VIII)
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-consciousness is an act and therefore implies will; intelligence is impossible except by and in a will, so freedom must be assumed as a ground of philosophy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spirit must in some sense dissolve identity to be conscious (alter et idem), which implies an active self-duplication — a volitional act rather than a passive state.

rubrics_metrics.name: The will as mediating principle and ground of transcendental philosophy (Thesis IX)
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary act of self-duplication (will) is the mediate principle of every science and the immediate principle of transcendental philosophy; it supplies the highest principle of knowing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These theses are confined to the subjective pole; the will/self-duplication functions as the source and accompanying form in all individual acts of intellect and perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transcendental philosophy seeks the last principle within our knowing (Thesis X)
rubrics_metrics.description: The transcendental philosopher asks what is the ultimate principle in our knowing itself — the last beyond which we cannot pass — treating the act of self-consciousness as the source and principle of possible knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle is sought within the sphere of knowing and may be something which, for us, cannot itself be known except as the act or form of our knowing; whether anything beyond it exists is to be decided by the result.
